description: Visual grammar first; subjects map to applicable operations. Each family holds at least five inspected reference images. Runtime loads only selected images and instructions.

selectionPolicy.fallback: No credible match: no unrelated default reference.
selectionPolicy.pacing: Complete the understanding plan, script and visual instructions before deriving runtime.
selectionPolicy.usage: Attributed internal references only. Generate original scene assets; do not insert creator screenshots, logos, watermarks or captions into output.
selectionPolicy.evidence: Frames and illustrations inspected for static composition. Continuous motion, narration and learner comprehension are not inferred from still images.

families.label: Analytical canvas
families.summary: Flat mathematical objects, curves, local magnification and transformations. Algebra and calculus share this visual grammar.
families.instructions: Use a quiet high-contrast mathematical canvas. Make relationships visible with curves, areas, anchored vectors, matching colors and retained before-states. Algebra and calculus belong together when the visual operation is the same; do not impose a separate decorative theme. Start with one concrete quantity, show what changes, then explain why. Zoom into a local change while retaining its location in the larger picture. Introduce each axis, scale and symbol before use. Equations appear only when needed for intuition or calculation; attach every term to an established object. Build dense reference compositions in separate explanatory beats. Never infer pacing from a still or source runtime.

families.label: Spatial geometry and higher-dimensional views
families.summary: Depth, basis frames, projection, surfaces and transparent solids; explicit representations of 4D.
families.instructions: Use genuine spatial structure: perspective, restrained lighting, depth ordering, occlusion and selectively transparent surfaces. Establish axes, frame and camera before movement; retain an orientation landmark. Distinguish moving the camera from changing the object. Match object identities across original and projected views. For four-dimensional objects, explicitly name the projection or slice into three/two dimensions and the missing coordinate; explain distortions and information loss. A 3D rendering is not a literal view of 4D. Teach the lower-dimensional analogy before the higher-dimensional construction. Use equations only to name an already understood relation or perform the necessary calculation.

references.title: Principal Component Analysis (PCA)

limitations: Do not import the formula or the phrase “information preserved” without defining the quantity. For PCA, explain centered data, unit direction and variance before the optimization objective. One point-to-line picture is not a complete PCA explanation.

families.label: Discrete state and information flow
families.summary: Items, trees, networks, arrays and relation matrices with stable identity and visible state changes.
families.instructions: Represent discrete entities with legible cards, nodes, cells or token columns. Keep positions and identity stable while highlighting one state change or dependency. Explain what a link carries and its direction before animating information through it. Trace one small input by hand before expanding the system. Show the rule, its local consequence, and the retained previous state. Use matrices for pairwise relationships, not as decorative blocks of numbers. Neural-network schematics and algorithms share this grammar when showing computation; geometric embeddings instead belong to spatial geometry. Dense networks are late recaps, never opening frames. Perspective may group data but must not imply physical space.

families.label: Populations, distributions and uncertainty
families.summary: Repeated cases, filtering, proportionate area and histograms connect individuals to aggregate behavior.
families.instructions: Begin with an individual case and define what one mark represents. Build populations from repeated marks; preserve excluded cases dimly during filtering. Translate counts into area or bins with explicit one-to-one correspondence and labeled denominators. Distinguish probability, sample frequency and density. Introduce bins, axes, normalization and changed scales before using them. Compare one sample with an ensemble, then show how aggregation changes the distribution. Never replace an unfamiliar population with a finished bell curve without explaining the bridge. Use formulas only after their populations and quantities are visible. Population biology uses this style when counting organisms, not molecular machinery.

references.observed: Ten grey book-holding figures occupy one column; two hundred green wheat-holding figures fill twenty columns. Braces label group sizes 10 and 200. Uniform icon size makes the base-rate imbalance visible.
limitations: Do not copy profession icons into unrelated subjects. Establish one mark equals one case.

families.label: Molecular bodies and mechanisms
families.summary: Complex biological assemblies, molecular chains, selective transparency and context-to-interaction scale changes.
families.instructions: Use recognizable complex molecular bodies, chains and assemblies with meaningful 3D structure. Do not substitute generic spheres or flat labeled boxes for a molecular mechanism. Choose scientifically justified structural detail and explain what the representation omits; do not invent atomic coordinates. Establish each participant, its role and relative scale before revealing interaction. Preserve chain and subunit identity across folding, binding and assembly. Use cutaways, translucency or an exploded view to reveal the active site while retaining outer context. Reduce background contrast to isolate the current action. Make proximity, contact, conformational change and resulting function visible in successive beats. Return from the local mechanism to its biological consequence. Molecular detail supports explanation; it does not prove biological correctness.
